draft.title: De facto relationships
card: A de facto relationship is a couple who live together as a couple on a genuine domestic basis without being married. They can be of the same sex or different sexes.
A court looks at the whole relationship to decide if it is de facto. It considers things such as how long they lived together, whether they shared money and a home, and how others saw them.

Under the Family Law Act 1975, a de facto couple who separate can ask the court to divide their property and to order maintenance (financial support). These are most of the same rights that married couples have.
A de facto couple do not need a marriage certificate or a divorce. The law looks at how they lived, not at a formal ceremony.
draft.remember: Living together as a couple can give most of the same separation rights as marriage, because the law looks at how the couple lived.

a.q: Why can Priya and Tom, who lived together for five years without marrying, ask a court to divide their property when they separate?
opts: Their shared life can make them a de facto couple
They signed a marriage certificate after moving in
They must first get a divorce before a court can act
They are treated as married once they share a home
a.why: The Family Law Act 1975 gives de facto couples most of the same rights on separation, based on how they lived together. They did not marry, so a marriage certificate is not the reason. A divorce is not needed either, because they were never married.
a.clue: The court looks at how the couple lived, not at a ceremony.

b.q: Mia and Jack have lived together in Dubbo for three years, share a home and bills, and are known as a couple. They separate. Which statement is correct?
opts: Mia can ask a court for property division and maintenance
Mia has no rights, because they never married
Mia must first obtain a divorce from Jack
Mia has rights only if they have a child together
b.why: A court can find that Mia and Jack were in a de facto relationship from how they lived. She can then seek property division and maintenance under the Family Law Act 1975. A divorce is not needed, because they were never married.
b.clue: Think about what the court examines: the couple's life together.

a.best: Their shared life can make them a de facto couple

b.best: Mia can ask a court for property division and maintenance

problems.detail: The card implies any separating de facto couple can ask for property orders or maintenance. Under the Family Law Act 1975 (s 90SB), the court can usually make these orders only if the relationship lasted at least 2 years in total, or there is a child, or one partner made substantial contributions, or the relationship was registered. This gateway is core HSC content and should be mentioned.
The right option is the only one with a qualifier ('can make'). The distractors are flat, absolute claims, so a student could pick it without knowing the idea.

proposal.title: De facto relationships
card: A de facto relationship is a couple who live together on a genuine domestic basis without being married. They can be of the same sex or different sexes.
A court looks at the whole relationship to decide if it is de facto. It considers things such as how long they lived together, whether they shared money and a home, and how others saw them.

Under the Family Law Act 1975, de facto partners who separate can ask the court to divide their property and to order maintenance (financial support). These are most of the same rights that married couples have.

The court can usually make these orders only if one gateway test is met: the relationship lasted at least 2 years in total, there is a child of the relationship, one partner made substantial contributions, or the relationship was registered.
proposal.remember: Living together as a couple can give most of the separation rights of marriage, usually once a gateway test, such as 2 years together, is met.

a.q: Ana and Leo lived together as a couple for 8 months. They have no child, never registered the relationship and neither made substantial contributions. They separate. Can a court usually make property orders?
opts: No, because none of the gateway tests is met
Yes, because they lived together as a couple
Yes, because any separating couple can apply
No, because the law covers only married couples
a.why: De facto partners can seek property orders, but usually only if a gateway test is met. Ana and Leo were together under 2 years, with no child, registration or substantial contributions, so none is met. Living together as a couple is not enough on its own.
a.clue: Check each gateway test against their situation.

b.q: Mia and Jack lived together as a couple in Dubbo for 18 months and had a baby together. They never married or registered the relationship. They separate. Which statement is correct?
opts: The court can make orders, because they have a child
The court cannot, because they were together under 2 years
The court cannot, because they never married
The court can, but only once they register the relationship
b.why: The gateway tests are alternatives, so meeting any one is enough. Mia and Jack have a child of the relationship, so the court can make property and maintenance orders even though they were together under 2 years. Registration is just one of the tests, not a requirement.
b.clue: Does a couple need to meet every gateway test, or just one?

The card presents substantial contributions alone as enough, which overstates that test. Add 'and not making an order would be seriously unjust' or similar.
